newsitem.title: JAPAN: Russia seeks more Japanese direct investment.
newsitem.headline: Russia seeks more Japanese direct investment.

text.p: Russian Deputy Prime Minister Boris Nemtsov called on Monday for more direct Japanese investment in his country, particularly in Russia's Far East, and said the priority was energy-related projects.
Nemtsov, who arrived in Tokyo on Monday for a three-day visit, told Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda that Russia also wanted Japan to invest in its lumber, automobile and home electronics sectors.

The visit highlights the growing commercial courtship between Russia, with its vast energy reserves, and Tokyo, which is poor in natural resources but has the cash that Moscow needs to revitalise its industries.

A Japanese Foreign Ministry official, briefing reporters about the meeting with Ikeda, said Nemtsov, who also holds Russia's fuel and energy portfolio, expressed particular interest in direct investment in Russia's Far East, site of rich gas and oil reserves.
Russia is also keen to jump-start some joint business projects which Japanese industry sources say have been hampered by funding problems and red tape.
Key Japanese projects in Russia include the development of gas and oil fields off Sakhalin island in Russia's Far East.
Japanese firms are keen to push on with the ventures which they see as a means of diversifying Japan's sources of energy imports, now predominantly from the Middle East.
Japanese companies have stakes in the $12 billion Sakhalin I project and the $10 billion Sakhalin II project.
Sakhalin I is believed to have reserves of some 2.5 billion barrels of crude and more than 15 trillion cubic feet of natural gas. Production is due to start around 2001 to 2002.
But Japanese industry sources have said that red tape is thwarting Japanese investment in the area.

Nemtsov said that he was aware that local authorities have at times been slow in implementing government decisions such as rules on taxation. Under existing Sakhalin production-sharing agreements, companies are responsible only for taxes on profits if and when oil starts flowing, but some have complained of levies at the local or regional level.
The Russian minister said that such problems have been resolved at the regional level.
Nemtsov also told Reuters in an interview that Russia guarantees tax-free conditions for Sakhalin oil deals, re-affirming a pledge made by Moscow last year.
In a fresh sign of closer ties, Japan and Russia signed an agreement on Monday for the first tranche of a $500 million loan that Japan originally pledged in October 1991.
The loan was initially earmarked for humanitarian programmes, but Russia asked that it also be applied to commercial projects and Monday's disbursement includes money for an automobile project.

Japanese government officials said Japan's trade with Russia totals roughly $5 billion a year, while its direct investments in Russia stood at about $227 million, an amount Nemtsov described as insufficient.
Nemtsov is due to pay a courtesy call on Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto on Tuesday and will also meet Japan's trade minister and business leaders.
